content:
Apple has filed new documents in its lawsuit against OpenAI, continuing to push for accelerated discovery. In today's filing, Apple said that based on a preliminary forensic examination of the laptop used by former engineer Chang Liu, it uncovered new "stunning evidence."

Apple first filed the lawsuit in July of this year, accusing a former employee of stealing trade secrets for OpenAI's benefit. A few weeks later, Apple sought a temporary restraining order and asked the court to expedite discovery, including obtaining documents early and taking depositions from key OpenAI employees and executives. Apple reiterated last week the need to accelerate the process. OpenAI has moved to dismiss the lawsuit.

As previously reported, Chang Liu is one of the named defendants in Apple's lawsuit. Liu was a senior systems electrical engineer at Apple and left in January to join OpenAI. The lawsuit alleges that Liu exploited a security vulnerability to download confidential engineering files after his departure.

In today's filing, Apple said Liu's counsel had previously turned over the MacBook Liu used after leaving the company. Apple said the "preliminary forensic analysis" of the MacBook revealed four points, quoted from Apple's filing as follows:

  • Mr. Liu not only downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic, but used it in his work at OpenAI;
  • Mr. Liu and others at OpenAI were far from unaware of his unauthorized access to Apple's third-party cloud storage; on the contrary, they were fully aware of the access;
  • After learning of Apple's internal investigation into him, Mr. Liu sent instructions to an OpenAI colleague to destroy evidence, and the colleague confirmed they would comply; and
  • Mr. Liu used a tool during his time at OpenAI with the same name as an engineering application Apple uses internally for development work.

Apple alleges that Liu ran a circuit schematic simulation in March using LTspice (an electrical engineering tool). In a message around the same time, Liu said his AI "agent" had learned to run LTspice and review the results.

Apple noted that when trade secret information is fed into an AI agent or model that learns from it, the learning process "may cause a persistent and irreversible dissemination of the trade secrets."

Apple said the defendants chose not to examine the laptop, opting instead to "argue that the device's data could rebut the allegations."

In addition, Apple learned of Liu's use of the schematic because he opened the file on a Mac mini, which was then synced via iCloud to the MacBook he took from Apple. Apple is now also seeking that Mac mini.
